title: Starting again
intro: Four people describe changing career in their thirties.

sections.heading: Marta, from accountant to chef
sections.text: After eight years of spreadsheets, I was bored rather than unhappy, and I kept wondering whether I would regret never trying the thing I loved. So at thirty I resigned and enrolled on a cookery course, and six months later I was working in a restaurant kitchen. My salary halved overnight, which took some getting used to. Nothing in accountancy had prepared me for the heat, the noise or the speed of a busy service, and for the first few weeks I was terrified of getting an order wrong while the experienced cooks were watching. What keeps me going is something I never had in an office: when a plate comes back empty, or a customer asks to thank the chef, I know straight away that I have done a good job.

sections.heading: James, from teacher to software developer
sections.text: I taught maths for nine years, and for the last two of them I spent most evenings and weekends learning to code through online courses. It was exhausting, but I couldn't afford to give up my salary until I was sure I could find work as a developer. Eventually a small start-up took a chance on me, and I have never looked back financially: I now earn considerably more than I did in the classroom. Oddly enough, I don't miss the teaching itself as much as I expected. What I do miss is the staffroom and, above all, the students. There is plenty of banter in an office, but nothing quite compares to the energy of a class of teenagers.

sections.heading: Lena, from lawyer to carpenter
sections.text: When I announced that I was leaving my law firm to train as a carpenter, my parents were horrified. They had paid for my degree and thought I was throwing my education away, and it took them a long time to come round to the idea. At thirty-five I started an apprenticeship alongside a group of sixteen-year-olds, who found it hilarious that someone my age was learning to use a chisel. I love the physical satisfaction of making something that will last, but I would be lying if I said I never missed the law. Constructing an argument, finding the weak point in the other side's case: that kind of mental challenge is hard to replace.

sections.heading: Raj, from engineer to nurse
sections.text: For years I designed bridges and enjoyed it. Then my father became seriously ill, and I spent months at his bedside watching the nurses who cared for him. It made me question whether the work I was doing really mattered to me as much as I had thought. A year later, I gave up my job to study nursing full-time, in a class whose members ranged from school-leavers to people in their fifties. To my surprise, my engineering background has been genuinely valuable. Nursing involves constant problem-solving under pressure, and the habit of checking every detail twice has served me well. The shift work is exhausting, but I have never felt more certain that I am in the right place.

items.statement: I was considerably older than the others I trained with.
items.hint: Who trained alongside teenagers?
items.explanation: Lena started her apprenticeship at thirty-five 'alongside a group of sixteen-year-olds'. Raj's class included people of all ages.

items.statement: I accepted a considerably lower income in order to make the change.
items.hint: Whose salary 'halved overnight'?
items.explanation: Marta's salary 'halved overnight'. James, by contrast, now earns more than before.

items.statement: Watching other people at work made me rethink my own career.
items.hint: Who spent months observing professionals caring for a relative?
items.explanation: Raj watched the nurses caring for his father, and it made him question whether his own work really mattered to him.

items.statement: I prepared for my new career without giving up my old job.
items.hint: Who studied in the evenings while still working?
items.explanation: James learned to code in the evenings and at weekends because he couldn't afford to give up his salary. The others left their jobs first.

items.statement: I still sometimes long for the intellectual demands of my previous work.
items.hint: Who misses constructing arguments?
items.explanation: Lena says the 'mental challenge' of the law is hard to replace. James, by contrast, doesn't miss the teaching itself.

items.statement: At the beginning, I was anxious about making mistakes in front of more experienced colleagues.
items.hint: Who was 'terrified' while others were watching?
items.explanation: Marta was terrified of getting an order wrong 'while the experienced cooks were watching'.

items.statement: Habits I developed in my previous career have proved useful in my new one.
items.hint: Whose old background turned out to be 'genuinely valuable'?
items.explanation: Raj's habit of 'checking every detail twice' from engineering has served him well in nursing. Marta says accountancy had not prepared her at all.

items.statement: What I miss most about my old job is the company of the people there.
items.hint: Who misses the staffroom and the students?
items.explanation: James misses 'the staffroom and, above all, the students', not the teaching itself.

items.statement: I value the immediate evidence that I have done my work well.
items.hint: Who knows 'straight away' that the job was well done?
items.explanation: When a plate comes back empty, Marta knows 'straight away' that she has done a good job.

items.statement: People close to me disapproved of my decision at first.
items.hint: Whose parents were 'horrified'?
items.explanation: Lena's parents were horrified and took a long time to 'come round to the idea'.

title: A month without a smartphone
intro: Four people describe giving up their smartphones for a month.

sections.heading: Chloe, university student
sections.text: I signed up for the challenge partly as a joke, but it turned out to be one of the most useful things I did all year. The practical side was harder than I expected. Without a map in my pocket, I got hopelessly lost twice in a city I thought I knew well, and I had to ask strangers for directions like a tourist. My friends were less than impressed, too; several of them grumbled that organising anything with me had become impossible because they could never reach me. On the other hand, I suddenly had hours to spare in the evenings, so I borrowed my flatmate's old guitar and started teaching myself to play. I still practise most nights, months after the experiment ended.

sections.heading: Mike, sales manager
sections.text: My job depends on being available, so I compromised and used an old mobile that could only make calls. Even so, the first week was horrible. I kept reaching for my pocket, I felt restless and irritable, and I was convinced I was missing out on what everyone else was saying. Gradually, though, the anxiety faded. The most dramatic change was at night: without a screen in bed, I was falling asleep within minutes and waking up properly rested for the first time in years. My wife noticed the difference before I did. She said it was like having a conversation with someone who was actually in the room, rather than half of him.

sections.heading: Aiko, freelance photographer
sections.text: As a freelancer, my biggest fear was that clients would give up on me if I didn't reply to messages within minutes, and that I would be left without work. In fact, the opposite happened: an editor who had heard about the experiment contacted me by email and offered me a commission to photograph it. Without a phone to look at, I found myself noticing details of the city I had walked past a thousand times, from carvings above doorways to the way the light fell on the river in the early morning. I would love to say the experience changed me permanently, but within a week of the month ending, I was just as glued to my screen as before.

sections.heading: Daniel, retired teacher
sections.text: My grandson challenged me to do the month with him, and I agreed on the condition that he kept his side of the bargain. For me, the hardest part was the small empty moments, waiting at the bus stop or in a queue, when I would normally check the news. To fill the silence at home, I dug out the old radio from the attic and found myself listening to plays and documentaries every evening, just as I used to do when I was young. The biggest surprise, though, came at the end. My grandson told me that the best part had been our phone calls, because for once I had given him my full attention.

items.statement: I started to notice things I had always ignored.
items.hint: Who noticed details of a city they had walked past 'a thousand times'?
items.explanation: Aiko began noticing carvings above doorways and the light on the river, things she had always walked past.

items.statement: I had difficulty finding my way around.
items.hint: Who got lost and had to ask strangers for directions?
items.explanation: Chloe got 'hopelessly lost twice' without a map on her phone.

items.statement: I did the experiment together with a relative.
items.hint: Who was challenged by a family member to do it with them?
items.explanation: Daniel did the month together with his grandson. Mike's wife noticed a change, but she did not take part.

items.statement: I began to sleep much better.
items.hint: Who was falling asleep 'within minutes'?
items.explanation: Without a screen in bed, Mike was falling asleep quickly and waking up properly rested.

items.statement: I was afraid that the experiment would cost me work.
items.hint: Who feared clients would give up on them?
items.explanation: Aiko feared she 'would be left without work' if she didn't reply to clients quickly.

items.statement: Friends found it frustrating that they could not contact me.
items.hint: Whose friends 'grumbled'?
items.explanation: Chloe's friends complained that organising anything with her had become impossible because they could never reach her.

items.statement: I found the start of the experiment emotionally difficult.
items.hint: Who felt 'restless and irritable' in the first week?
items.explanation: Mike says the first week was 'horrible': he felt restless, irritable and anxious.

items.statement: I went back to a pastime I had enjoyed in the past.
items.hint: Who did something 'just as I used to do when I was young'?
items.explanation: Daniel started listening to the radio again, as he did when he was young. Chloe's guitar was something new for her.

items.statement: The experiment had no lasting effect on my behaviour.
items.hint: Who was 'just as glued to my screen as before' a week later?
items.explanation: Within a week of the month ending, Aiko was using her phone as much as before.

items.statement: I took up an activity that I have continued since.
items.hint: Who still practises something 'months after the experiment ended'?
items.explanation: Chloe started teaching herself the guitar and still practises most nights.

title: Start-ups on campus
intro: Four students describe setting up a business while at university.

sections.heading: Sofia, textbook-sharing app
sections.text: The idea came to me in my first year, when I realised I had spent more on textbooks than on food. I built a simple app that lets students borrow books from each other, and when I entered it in the university's enterprise competition, it won first prize, which gave me enough money to pay a developer. The difficult part was everything else. Running a business in the middle of a degree meant constant juggling, and in my second year my marks dropped badly because I was answering customer emails instead of revising. Even so, my message to other students is simple: don't wait until you graduate. University is the safest place there is to try something and fail.

sections.heading: Tom, vintage clothing shop
sections.text: This is actually my second business. The first, selling phone cases, collapsed within three months because I had ordered far too much stock. This time I started small, with two hundred pounds of savings and a few bags of clothes from charity shops. My parents lent me their van at weekends so I could visit car-boot sales, and my sister helped me photograph everything. What really made the difference, though, was Instagram. Once a couple of well-known accounts shared my posts, orders started arriving faster than I could pack them. I still study full-time, but the shop now pays my rent.

sections.heading: Yusuf, campus food delivery
sections.text: I set up a delivery service for students with a friend from my course, and for the first year everything went brilliantly. We had more orders than we could handle and were thinking about expanding to other universities. Then we fell out over money, as so many business partners do. He thought he was doing more of the work; I thought the same about myself. Because we had never written anything down, there was no way of settling who owned what, and in the end I bought him out at a price I could barely afford. If there is one lesson I would pass on, it is to agree everything on paper before you start, even with your best friend.

sections.heading: Nina, online tutoring platform
sections.text: My platform matches school pupils with university students who can tutor them online. In the early days I nearly gave up, because I couldn't persuade schools to take me seriously. It was one of my economics lecturers who suggested I stop selling to schools and go directly to parents instead. That single piece of advice changed everything. Within a year we had hundreds of families signed up, and today twelve students from my university work for the company as tutors and organisers. Being able to offer them flexible, well-paid work that fits around their timetable is one of the things I am proudest of.

items.statement: A previous business venture of mine was unsuccessful.
items.hint: Whose first business 'collapsed within three months'?
items.explanation: Tom's first business, selling phone cases, collapsed because he ordered too much stock. Nina nearly gave up, but her business did not fail.

items.statement: Advice from a member of the teaching staff transformed my approach.
items.hint: Who took a lecturer's suggestion?
items.explanation: One of Nina's lecturers suggested selling to parents instead of schools, and 'that single piece of advice changed everything'.

items.statement: I used prize money to get my business started.
items.hint: Who won a competition?
items.explanation: Sofia's app won first prize in the university's enterprise competition, which paid for a developer.

items.statement: A disagreement ended a partnership.
items.hint: Who fell out with a business partner?
items.explanation: Yusuf and his friend 'fell out over money', and he ended up buying his partner out.

items.statement: Relatives gave me practical support.
items.hint: Whose parents and sister helped out?
items.explanation: Tom's parents lent him their van and his sister helped him photograph the clothes.

items.statement: My academic results suffered because of the business.
items.hint: Whose marks 'dropped badly'?
items.explanation: Sofia's marks dropped in her second year because she was answering emails instead of revising. Tom still studies full-time without mentioning problems.

items.statement: I am proud of the employment opportunities I have created.
items.hint: Who now gives work to twelve students?
items.explanation: Nina says offering students flexible, well-paid work is one of the things she is proudest of.

items.statement: I regret not having formalised an arrangement.
items.hint: Who had 'never written anything down'?
items.explanation: Because Yusuf and his partner had not written anything down, they could not settle who owned what; he advises agreeing everything on paper.

items.statement: Online publicity led to a sudden increase in sales.
items.hint: Whose orders took off after popular accounts shared their posts?
items.explanation: When well-known Instagram accounts shared Tom's posts, orders arrived faster than he could pack them.

items.statement: I would encourage students to start a business while still studying.
items.hint: Who says 'don't wait until you graduate'?
items.explanation: Sofia tells other students not to wait until they graduate, because university is the safest place to try and fail.

title: My first marathon
intro: Four runners describe their first marathon.

sections.heading: Elena
sections.text: I trained using an app on my phone that told me exactly how far and how fast to run each day, and for four months everything went to plan. Then, three weeks before the race, I twisted my knee on a forest path. For a few days I was sure my marathon was over before it had begun, and it was only thanks to a patient physiotherapist that I made it to the start line at all. I ran far more slowly than I had hoped, but I will never forget the crowds. Every time I felt like giving up, someone I had never met would shout my name from the pavement, and somehow my legs kept moving.

sections.heading: Ben
sections.text: I signed up for the marathon in memory of a friend who died of cancer, and the sponsorship I collected went to the hospice that looked after him. Knowing how many people had donated made it impossible to drop out, which was just as well, because at around thirty kilometres I hit what runners call the wall. My legs simply refused to cooperate, and for two or three kilometres I had no choice but to walk while hundreds of people overtook me. Eventually I managed to start jogging again and crossed the line in just under five hours. It was the hardest thing I have ever done, and I'm already planning next year's race.

sections.heading: Grace
sections.text: Two years ago, I couldn't run for a bus. I was overweight, I smoked, and my idea of exercise was walking to the fridge. A health scare changed all that. I gave up cigarettes, changed my diet and started with short jogs around the park, often in the dark so that nobody would see me. The turning point was joining a local running club. Having people who expected me to turn up on a Tuesday evening, and who celebrated every small improvement, kept me going through the winter. Finishing the marathon wasn't really about the race; it was proof of how much my life had changed.

sections.heading: Omar
sections.text: I had been a competitive cyclist for years, so I assumed a marathon would be fairly straightforward. That was my first mistake. Running uses completely different muscles, and my fitness on the bike counted for much less than I had imagined. My second mistake came on the day itself. Full of adrenaline, I set off with the leading club runners and covered the first ten kilometres far faster than I had ever trained. By halfway my legs had turned to stone, and the final hour was agony, although I refused to stop running. I'm glad I can say I've done it, but once is definitely enough.

items.statement: My background in a different sport misled me.
items.hint: Who thought their fitness from another sport would be enough?
items.explanation: Omar assumed his years of cycling would make the marathon straightforward, but his fitness 'counted for much less' than he imagined.

items.statement: An injury almost stopped me from taking part.
items.hint: Who twisted a knee three weeks before?
items.explanation: Elena twisted her knee and only reached the start line thanks to a physiotherapist.

items.statement: Completing the race showed how much my way of life had changed.
items.hint: Who used to smoke and never exercise?
items.explanation: For Grace, finishing the marathon was 'proof of how much my life had changed'.

items.statement: I took part in order to raise money for a good cause.
items.hint: Who collected sponsorship for a hospice?
items.explanation: Ben ran in memory of a friend and his sponsorship went to the hospice that cared for him.

items.statement: I relied on technology to plan my training.
items.hint: Who followed an app?
items.explanation: Elena trained with an app that told her how far and how fast to run each day.

items.statement: I started the race at a speed I could not keep up.
items.hint: Who set off with the leading runners?
items.explanation: Omar ran the first ten kilometres faster than he had ever trained and paid for it later.

items.statement: At one point I was unable to run.
items.hint: Who had 'no choice but to walk'?
items.explanation: After hitting 'the wall', Ben had to walk for two or three kilometres. Omar suffered but 'refused to stop running'.

items.statement: Other people's expectations motivated me during training.
items.hint: Who had people expecting them to turn up every week?
items.explanation: Grace's running club expected her to turn up on Tuesday evenings, which kept her going through the winter.

items.statement: Encouragement from people watching helped me continue.
items.hint: Who heard strangers shouting their name?
items.explanation: Elena says strangers shouting her name from the pavement kept her legs moving.

items.statement: I have no plans to repeat the experience.
items.hint: Who says 'once is definitely enough'?
items.explanation: Omar is glad he did it, but 'once is definitely enough'. Ben, by contrast, is already planning next year's race.
